title: Encryption operational readiness and BYO-KMS workshop - Zenith Capital
summary: High-level security review focused on encryption at rest/in-transit, BYO-KMS/HSM integration patterns, operational runbooks for key rotation and emergency key revocation, and audit log requirements for Zenith's private deployment. Agreed to share SOC2 docs, design diagram, and schedule a short proof-of-concept with test keys.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-09 15:00 UTC | Duration: 62 minutes | Location: Zoom | Recording: enabled
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (CS), Daniel Reed (Zenith), Maya Chen (Zenith), Tom Alvarez (Zenith), Rita Gonzales (Zenith)

[00:00] Alex Morgan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call - I think we have the right folks for the BYO KMS and encryption runbook discussion.
[00:18] Daniel Reed: Yep, sounds good. We want to make sure the design meets our controls for key custody and zero access from hosted components.
[00:28] Priya Kapoor: Great, so we'll cover integration patterns first—cloud provider KMS with IAM, KMIP-based HSMs, and an offline key escrow flow. We'll also go through rotation, revocation and audit logs.
[00:45] Maya Chen: One of our non-negotiables is we need key material never to be exportable from our HSMs and the platform must support BYO-KMS with HSM-backed keys.
[01:05] Alex Morgan: Understood. Redwood supports both BYOK via KMS API and HSM via KMIP or a managed HSM flow. One thing to note, we use envelope encryption at rest—so model weight blobs and KV caches are wrapped with a tenant key and the tenant key is wrapped by the master key you control.
[01:30] Tom Alvarez: Can you repeat the envelope part? We heard 'envelop' — transcript sometimes says envelope as 'envelop'—
[01:36] Priya Kapoor: Sure. Envelope encryption means we keep a data encryption key (DEK) per volume or object which is used to encrypt the data. The DEK is then encrypted with your KEK (key encryption key) which resides in your KMS/HSM. So Redwood never stores your unwrapped master key.
[02:12] Rita Gonzales: On the HSM side, our vendor requires KMIP and they want to rotate keys every 90 days. How does Redwood handle key rotation without causing downtime or losing access to cached KV state?
[02:30] Priya Kapoor: We do key rotation with multi-version support in the key registry. When a new KEK version is provisioned we rewrap DEKs lazily on access, and we maintain older KEK versions for decrypting existing objects for a configurable retention window. For hot KV caches we rely on prefix-aware caching and we persist wrapped DEKs — on first access after rotation we unwrap with the old KEK and rewrap with the new. That avoids mass re-encrypt.
[03:10] Daniel Reed: That sounds good, but can we get a clear runbook for emergency rotation — like if a key is suspected to be compromised? We need steps, who runs it, and how to roll back.
[03:26] Alex Morgan: Yes. We can provide a playbook. Quick summary: 1) Freeze writes to affected namespace, 2) provision new KEK version, 3) run rewrap job with accelerated concurrency, 4) validate via checksum and audit logs, 5) resume. For rollback, we keep previous KEK versions until tombstone and can revert. We'll include bench times in the doc.
[03:58] Speaker 2 (Jordan Lee): Also note our autoscaler and routing have fallback policies so if BYO-KMS endpoints are unreachable we can failover to a designated emergency key held in an out-of-band HSM in the customer's control — but that is a policy toggle and requires agreement.
[04:20] Maya Chen: Path to auditability is critical. We need immutable audit logs with both request/response and key lifecycle events, and logs should be exportable to our SIEM and retained for at least 3 years.
[04:36] Priya Kapoor: Redwood's platform emits structured audit events: KMS key ops, wrap/unwrap events, token issuance, tenant admin actions. We can stream to Splunk/Datadog or push to S3 in NDJSON. Events include requestor principal, IP, timestamp, operation, object id, and cryptographic material identifiers.
[05:08] Tom Alvarez: Are logs tamper-evident? We require tamper-evidence for compliance.
[05:15] Alex Morgan: We support append-only storage for audit logs and we can sign log batches server-side with a log signing key or integrate with your log signing HSM. We'll document the options.
[05:36] Daniel Reed: Network egress is another concern — we need to ensure key ops don't cross disallowed regions. Can Redwood route KMS calls to our VPC endpoint?
[05:48] Priya Kapoor: Yes — for private deployments we support VPC endpoints and private link. KMS traffic can be restricted to your dedicated subnet and we can run the control plane in your VPC for the BYO-KMS control plane interactions. For hosted customers we offer regional endpoints and CIDR allowlists.
[06:20] Rita Gonzales: For HSM onboarding, the vendor wants to see an HSM provisioning workflow. We prefer HSMs in FIPS 140-2 Level 3 mode.
[06:30] Priya Kapoor: We have an HSM onboarding checklist that outlines steps: initial key ceremony, operator roles, split knowledge, backup/escrow, and attestation verification. We'll share that checklist and include templates for key ceremony logs.
[06:52] Alex Morgan: We'll also provide our recommended operator RBAC mappings — who can rotate, who can list keys, who can approve emergency operations — and hooks for SSO/SAML with Just-in-Time role mapping.
[07:08] Maya Chen: Important: we require separation of duties. The person who can rotate keys shouldn't be the same who approves production rollouts.
[07:18] Priya Kapoor: That's standard. Our RBAC integrates with your IDP. We can map AD groups to Redwood roles and enforce MFA for key ops.
[07:45] Daniel Reed: Let's talk about in-transit encryption and TLS termination. We do not want plaintext model payloads leaving our VPC. Where does Redwood terminate TLS for model traffic?
[07:56] Alex Morgan: In private deployments, TLS is terminated at your perimeter or our sidecar within your VPC depending on configuration. We support mutual TLS and certificate rotation. For hosted mode, TLS terminates at our edge with TLS1.3 and we provide connection-level encryption.
[08:20] Tom Alvarez: If we choose hosted initially, how can we audit that data path?
[08:26] Priya Kapoor: We can provide packet-level telemetry summaries, connection metadata logs, and per-request trace IDs that map to certificate thumbprints. For compliance customers we recommend private deployment so termination and certs are under your control.
[08:50] Speaker 3 (Maya): A question about caching — you mentioned KV caches earlier. Are cached items at rest encrypted with the same DEKs and how are those keys managed?
[09:03] Priya Kapoor: Cached items are encrypted at rest using the same envelope method. For in-memory caches we also use secure enclaves and memory protections; for persisted caches the wrapped DEKs are persisted next to the object. When rehydrating from the cache we do an unwrap-verify-rewrap sequence if needed.
[09:38] Daniel Reed: What about ciphertext rotation? Do you maintain versions in object metadata?
[09:43] Priya Kapoor: Yes object metadata contains KEK version and wrapped DEK id so you can always determine which KEK to use to unwrap. We keep retention config for older KEK versions to satisfy decryption windows.
[10:05] Rita Gonzales: If we have a cross-region replication need, how do you ensure keys and payloads don't leave approved regions?
[10:15] Alex Morgan: We have region-aware key policies. You can configure routing rules so that certain tenants or datasets are pinned to specific regions, and KMS calls for those datasets must hit residency-enforced KMS endpoints. We'll show a reference policy for that.
[10:40] Tom Alvarez: We need to discuss proof of possession — how do we demonstrate that keys are actually in our HSM and not just software wrappers?
[10:50] Priya Kapoor: We support HSM attestation flows and can produce signed attestation statements from the HSM vendor. We can also run a challenge/response test during the POC where the HSM signs a nonce and Redwood verifies it.
[11:20] Daniel Reed: Can we do periodic key escrow with offline backups? Our compliance requires offline escrow with dual custodian signing.
[11:30] Alex Morgan: Yes, we support that. We bake in a key escrow process—backups can be encrypted with a separate escrow key and require split knowledge to access. We'll include templates for escrow logs and custody handoff.
[11:58] Maya Chen: A few practical questions on ops: what is expected of our SREs during onboarding and what autopilot tasks will Redwood take?
[12:08] Jordan Lee: From a CS perspective, Redwood handles runtime ops for the inference runtime, patching, and telemetry for the service. Your SREs will be responsible for KMS endpoints, HSM provisioning, network ACLs, and identity configuration. We'll collaborate on runbooks and run a joint run-through during POC.
[12:40] Priya Kapoor: One wrinkle — caching plus batching can mask key rotation latencies. We'll simulate traffic profiles in the POC to measure rewrap throughput. We'll also show how batching can be tuned to keep latency SLOs intact during mass rotations.
[13:05] Daniel Reed: Good. Also want to validate that Redwood never logs plaintext prompts or sensitive fields.
[13:12] Alex Morgan: Redwood has configurable PII scrubbing at ingest. We can redact or tokenise fields before storage and the default for enterprise is to not persist raw prompts unless you opt in. We'll document how that works end-to-end.
[13:38] Tom Alvarez: About legal chain — do you provide an attestation that keys were never held by Redwood staff? We need language for our contracts.
[13:47] Alex Morgan: We can provide contractual language and a technical attestation describing that unwrapped keys are never present in Redwood-managed storage and that access is controlled through KMS calls to your HSM. Legal can follow-up; I'll include a starter clause.
[14:08] Maya Chen: OK let's run a quick hypothetical exercise: keys compromised, high severity. Walk us through the emergency plan end-to-end.
[14:18] Priya Kapoor: (walkthrough) 1) Detection & triage — customer creates incident and toggles freeze, 2) Redwood disables write path and moves reads to read-only state, 3) Provision replacement KEK and push to KMS, 4) Start coordinated rewrap with audit logging, 5) Validate via checksums, 6) Re-enable writes, 7) Post-mortem and rotate any dependent keys such as session tokens. We'll share a granular playbook.
[15:02] Speaker 2 (Jordan): During that process we can also enable increased logging verbosity and snapshot logs to WORM storage for forensic purposes.
[15:20] Daniel Reed: Do you have metrics on how long large-scale rewraps take? If we have a terabyte-scale model store.
[15:30] Priya Kapoor: We'll collect baseline numbers in the POC but typical rewrap throughput depends on concurrency and HSM unwrap latencies. With HSM that has hardware acceleration it can be X ops per second — we'll provide numbers and a benchmark sheet.
[16:00] Alex Morgan: We'll attach a benchmark spreadsheet. (link: https://redwood.example.com/zenith-keys-benchmark)
[16:15] Maya Chen: A question on key deletion: do you support secure deletion and key tombstoning aligned to our retention policy?
[16:25] Priya Kapoor: Yes. Keys can be scheduled for deletion with a configurable hold window. Tombstoning marks keys unusable but retains artifacts for audit. Secure deletion procedures vary by HSM vendor, but we will include vendor-specific instructions.
[16:50] Tom Alvarez: Can Redwood integrate with our central secrets manager for issuing short-lived credentials to operators?
[16:57] Alex Morgan: We support integration with HashiCorp Vault and AWS Secrets Manager. We can mint short-lived creds for operator jobs via an ephemeral token exchange.
[17:20] Rita Gonzales: For the POC, we expect to provision an HSM in our test environment. What's the minimum setup?
[17:27] Priya Kapoor: Minimal POC: 1 HSM or managed HSM instance, VPC peering or private link, sample dataset with non-production prompts, and an IDP test account. We'll provide a checklist.
[17:55] Daniel Reed: Great. Any concerns about latency impact from KMIP HSM unwraps? We might need sub-100ms token latency for some flows.
[18:08] Priya Kapoor: KMIP unwraps can add latency; common pattern is to cache DEKs in a secure local cache and only call HSM on key load/rotation. For per-request crypto we use tokenization to avoid HSM calls in the hot path. We'll show numbers.
[18:40] Alex Morgan: We'll include recommended caching TTLs and eviction policies.
[18:50] Maya Chen: On compliance evidence, we need a mapping of Redwood controls to our SOC2 and ISO requirements.
[18:58] Alex Morgan: We'll send a controls matrix that maps Redwood features to SOC2/ISO clauses and evidence artifacts.
[19:15] Tom Alvarez: One more thing — can we run a periodic attestations job where the HSM signs a digest of the active key roster and we compare it to the registry?
[19:25] Priya Kapoor: Yes, we support signed key roster snapshots. We'll include a sample script in the repo.
[19:40] Speaker 4 (Maya): A small nit — sometimes Fireflies transcript messes up acronyms. I heard 'kay vee' earlier, that's KV cache.
[19:47] Alex Morgan: Yep, KV cache.
[19:55] Daniel Reed: Ok let's recap actions, then plan the POC date.
[20:02] Alex Morgan: Recap: Alex sends SOC2 and HSM checklist; Priya drafts BYO-KMS architecture; Rita supplies network constraints; Zenith confirms POC participants. Proposed POC week of May 20th.
[20:20] Jordan Lee: I'll coordinate invites and the shared folder — link: https://redwood.example.com/zenith-poc-docs
[20:30] Maya Chen: Thanks. We're good to proceed.
[20:34] Alex Morgan: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up by Tuesday with the docs.

(Transcript continues with minor Q&A and clarifications until 62:00)

[61:10] Tom Alvarez: One last quick ask — can we have sample contractual language for key custody?
[61:20] Alex Morgan: Yes, legal will send a starter clause.
[61:34] Meeting end: 16:02 UTC
